questions.q: Why can a backup policy look completely correctly configured in the portal while the actual backups have been failing for weeks?
options: Backup policies cannot actually fail once they are created
The portal always shows a red warning the moment any backup job fails
Azure deletes a backup policy automatically the first time a job fails
A backup job can fail for reasons unrelated to the policy itself, like an unresponsive agent or a permission change, and the policy's configuration doesn't reflect that
questions.explain: The policy existing and looking correct is a different claim from the backup job actually completing successfully — the two can diverge silently.

questions.q: Why does the script use a rolling 24-hour window (-From (Get-Date).AddHours(-24) -To (Get-Date)) instead of a fixed date?
options: Because -From and -To are required parameters with no other valid values
Because Azure Backup only stores 24 hours of job history total
So the script only runs once per year
So it always checks the most recent day's activity regardless of when the script actually runs
questions.explain: A rolling window relative to "now" means the script checks yesterday's backup activity correctly no matter what day or time it runs.

questions.q: Why does the script filter on Status -ne "Completed" instead of specifically matching Status -eq "Failed"?
options: -ne "Completed" and -eq "Failed" always return the exact same results
It makes the script run faster
It catches anything that didn't finish cleanly, including cancelled or stuck jobs, not just the one obvious failure status
Azure Backup jobs only ever have a status of Completed or Failed, nothing else
questions.explain: Filtering on anything not equal to Completed is broader than matching only Failed, catching other non-success states too, like cancelled or stuck jobs.

questions.q: Why is this backup-verification check deliberately a separate script from the backup job itself?
options: There is no real reason — it could just as easily be combined
Separate scripts run faster than combined ones
Azure does not allow a single script to both run a backup and check its status
If the check lived inside the same pipeline as the backup, a failure that broke the backup could just as easily break the check meant to catch it
questions.explain: Running the verification independently means a shared failure point can't take down both the backup and the thing checking on it at the same time.

questions.q: What is the real-world consequence this lesson warns about when a silently failing backup job goes unchecked?
options: The VM being backed up will shut down automatically
A real cause of data loss — discovering there's nothing recent to restore from only when a restore is actually needed
Nothing — a failed backup job has no real consequence
The subscription automatically gets billed extra for the failed job
questions.explain: A backup that's been silently failing for weeks means there's no recent recovery point, and that gap is only discovered during an actual incident, at the worst time.
